newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Virgin Express wants fight on equal terms.
newsitem.headline: Virgin Express wants fight on equal terms.

text.p: Richard Branson's Virgin Express regional airline on Thursday urged European governments to ensure that airlines can compete on equal terms in a deregulated market.

"The (Belgian) government needs to adopt policies that allow us to compete on a level playing field...on all components of our business...which is all we're asking for. We can be very successful here in Belgium," chief executive officer Jonathan Ornstein told Reuters in an interview.
The next package of air liberalisation measures to be introduced by the European Union in April should effectively complete deregulation of the market.
But Ornstein said that new airlines would be discouraged and carriers -- such as Brussels-based Virgin Express -- that are based in higher-cost European countries would be at a disadvantage.
"Sabena is talking about relocating (pilots). That is something we are certainly looking very hard at," Ornstein said.

Belgian flag-carrier Sabena, 49 percent owned by Swissair, wants to relocate pilots to avoid having to pay heavy Belgian social security charges and save up to two billion francs ($60 million) per year.

"It is very difficult to compete against British carriers when they immediately have the cost advantage because they have social costs that are 25 percent of what we pay and tax rates that are significantly lower," he said.
He said personal income tax rates were significantly lower, especially for high paid employees like pilots.
"(British airlines) can afford to pay people less because they net more money," he said.
Ornstein said Virgin Express was currently putting crews in England for overnight aircraft.
"The crews in England will cost (Virgin Express) about 40 percent less than the crews in Belgium. But they will take home more money," he said.
Ornstein predicted that deregulation would have a much bigger impact in Europe than it did in the United States.
"Europe is going to be by far the centrepiece of change," he said.

"I've lived through deregulation in the United States but here the impact is going to be even greater," said Ornstein, a former president and chief executive of Continental Airlines Inc's wholly-owned Continental Express Inc unit.

"Whether you had an operation in Oklahoma or the State of Washington did not make any difference, but here the differences are so greatly exacerbated that there is going to be a huge shakeout over the next five years," he said.

He again criticised the planned alliance between British Airways (BA) and AMR Corporation's American Airlines. "It would have a serious negative impact on worldwide travel. It would effectively create an incredibly powerful monopoly. It's so clearly anti-competitive," he said.
But he was convinced that low-cost carriers would emerge victors in the open air transport battle.
"It's a win-win situation, in the end by having a strong competitive enviroment, lower fares, more people fly, more planes are sold, more people are employed," he said.
